questionText: How do Where and Select work, and how should you chain them?
shortAnswer: Where filters elements by predicate; Select projects each element into a new shape. Chain Where-first (fewer items to project), keep predicates pure, and project to DTOs at API boundaries instead of leaking entities.
detailedAnswer: Where(Func<T, bool>) streams matching elements; Select(Func<T, TResult>) transforms each. Order matters for clarity and often performance: filter before projecting (projecting discarded items wastes work, especially with expensive mappings or EF-translated projections). Predicates must be pure — side effects in Where run unpredictably (deferred + re-enumeration) and break EF translation. Overloads with index (Where((x, i) => ...)) solve positional logic without manual counters. Select with index enables rank/row numbers. Project early to DTOs in APIs: orders.Select(o => new OrderDto(o.Id, o.Total)) trims payloads and detaches EF tracking concerns; for EF queries prefer Select over Include+entity when only a few columns are needed (projection generates tighter SQL). Null handling: Where(x => x != null) before member access, or null-conditional inside Select with a follow-up filter. Chaining style: one operation per line for debuggability; extract complex predicates to named static methods (testable, reusable, EF-translatable when expression-bodied and simple).
internalWorking: Where/Select return iterator state machines (no work until enumerated); chaining nests enumerators (each MoveNext pulls through the pipeline — single pass, O(1) extra memory). Against EF, the expression trees translate to SQL WHERE/SELECT (server-side); untranslatable method calls throw or client-evaluate (logged warning — read logs).
realWorldUsage: API list endpoints (filter + shape), report row building, ETL transforms, and UI view-model projection.
commonMistake: Side effects in predicates (logging/counters inside Where — runs 0..N times unpredictably), projecting before filtering (wasted mapping), and leaking entities instead of projecting DTOs (over-fetch + tracking + serialization cycles).
technicalConversation: Ask what the SQL looks like for their repository's Where+Select chain — projection-to-SQL-columns versus SELECT * + tracking is the EF maturity check.
interviewFollowUp: Why does filter-before-project matter more against a database than in memory?
keyTakeaway: Where narrows, Select shapes. Filter first, stay pure, project DTOs at boundaries.

questionText: What does SelectMany do, and when is flattening the right operation?
shortAnswer: SelectMany maps each element to a collection, then flattens all results into one sequence. Use it for parent→children fan-out (orders→lines), cross joins, and multi-level expansion — with an optional result selector to keep parent context.
detailedAnswer: Select gives one output per input (order → its lines collection = nested lists). SelectMany gives many outputs per input, concatenated: orders.SelectMany(o => o.Lines) yields every line of every order in one stream. The three-argument overload preserves context: orders.SelectMany(o => o.Lines, (o, l) => new { o.Customer, l.Sku }) — essential when the child alone loses meaning (which customer owns this line?). Query syntax expresses the same as a second from: from o in orders from l in o.Lines select .... Cross joins: a.SelectMany(_ => b) pairs every a with every b (cartesian — mind the explosion). Null children need care: SelectMany(o => o.Lines ?? Enumerable.Empty<Line>()) avoids NullReference on null collections (EF navigation version: filtered include or null-guard depending on provider translation). Versus nested foreach: same complexity, composable and lazy; versus Join: SelectMany navigates existing relationships, Join matches on keys. Empty parents contribute nothing (no empty groups — contrast GroupJoin/GroupBy which preserve keys).
internalWorking: SelectMany nests iterators (outer advances, inner drains) — single pass, O(1) extra memory. EF translates collection-navigation SelectMany to CROSS/OUTER APPLY or JOINs. The result selector compiles into the same iterator (no intermediate list).
realWorldUsage: Order→lines expansion, tenant→users fan-out, tag explosion for search indexing, test-matrix generation, and permission flattening (roles→claims).
commonMistake: Null child collections (guard or coalesce), losing parent context (use the result selector), and SelectMany over huge cross products without Take/bounds (cartesian explosions).
technicalConversation: Ask when they would use Join instead — key-based matching of unrelated sets versus navigating existing parent/child relationships is the dividing line.
interviewFollowUp: How does the result-selector overload change what you can express versus nested foreach with manual pairing?
keyTakeaway: SelectMany = map-to-many + flatten. Keep parent context with the result selector; guard null children.

questionText: How do you project to DTOs correctly with EF Core, and what should you avoid?
shortAnswer: Project with Select into DTO constructors/initializers inside the query so SQL returns only needed columns with no tracking. Avoid: materializing entities then mapping (over-fetch), client-side methods in Select (translation failure), and mapping after ToList when a projection would do.
detailedAnswer: The golden query: db.Orders.Where(...).Select(o => new OrderDto(o.Id, o.Customer.Name, o.Lines.Sum(l => l.Qty))).ToListAsync() — one round trip, tight SQL, no change tracking, no cycles. Rules: construct DTOs in the expression (constructors or initializers both translate); navigate relationships freely (translates to joins); compute aggregates in SQL (Sum/Count translate); keep method calls to translatable surface (string/decimal/DateTime members mostly; custom C# methods do NOT translate — precompute values into locals first, which become parameters). Avoid: ToList() then Select (full entities + tracking + N+1 risk), AutoMapper ProjectTo without configuration review (it works via expression mapping — fine when configured, opaque when not), and Select after AsNoTracking... (AsNoTracking is irrelevant once projecting — projections are never tracked; drop it). Nested collections project to List<T> inside (ToList in a sub-Select translates to correlated subqueries — fine at sane sizes; huge graphs need split queries). Test the SQL (ToQueryString in tests/dev) — projection bugs show as SELECT * or client-eval warnings.
internalWorking: The query pipeline binds Select to a SQL SELECT list; navigation becomes JOINs; aggregates become GROUP-less scalar subqueries or GROUP BY. Untranslatable nodes throw InvalidOperationException ('could not be translated') — fail fast, never silent wrong data (client-eval of the top-level projection is blocked by default in modern EF).
realWorldUsage: Every API list/detail endpoint, report queries, dropdown option lists, and dashboard aggregations.
commonMistake: Entity-then-map (SELECT * + tracking), custom methods inside Select (translation throw at runtime), and trusting ProjectTo blindly (review generated SQL once per query shape).
technicalConversation: Ask to see ToQueryString output for their hottest endpoint — SELECT * or N+1 patterns in the log settle the debate instantly.
interviewFollowUp: Why are projections never tracked, and what does that imply for update flows?
keyTakeaway: Select DTOs inside the query: tight SQL, no tracking, one trip. Precompute the untranslatable outside.

questionText: How do OrderBy, ThenBy, and custom comparers work together?
shortAnswer: OrderBy sorts by the primary key; ThenBy adds tiebreakers in order (each stable over the previous). Custom IComparer<T> passed to the comparer overloads controls non-default ordering like case-insensitive or natural sort.
detailedAnswer: Chaining: users.OrderBy(u => u.LastName).ThenBy(u => u.FirstName) — stable sorts compose (equal primaries keep ThenBy order; equal overall keeps original order — LINQ sorting is stable, unlike Array.Sort which is unstable introsort!). Descending variants per level (OrderByDescending/ThenByDescending). Custom order: OrderBy with an IComparer<T> overload (e.g. StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase), or key-projection tricks (OrderBy(u => u.Role == "Admin" ? 0 : 1) for pinned-first). Query syntax: orderby last, first — with descending keyword per key. EF translation: ORDER BY list server-side; untranslatable keys throw (precompute). Nulls: OrderBy puts nulls first (reference types) — add ?? sentinels for explicit placement. Performance: sorting is O(n log n) with key extraction per comparison — project cheap keys (avoid ToString in keys), sort before paging (stable paging needs deterministic order — always end with ThenBy(id)!), and push ORDER BY to the database over in-memory sorts of large sets. Reverse(): O(n) re-walk, not a re-sort — use for flipping already-sorted data only.
internalWorking: LINQ OrderBy is a stable mergesort-ish (actually a stable quicksort variant) buffering keys; ThenBy chains comparers (CompoundComparer). EF emits ORDER BY a, b. Stability guarantee is documented for LINQ-to-Objects — code depending on it is safe, unlike Array.Sort.
realWorldUsage: Sorted tables, leaderboards, deterministic API paging, dropdown ordering, and report grouping headers.
commonMistake: Multiple OrderBy (each re-sorts — later wins, earlier wasted; use ThenBy), missing final tiebreak (nondeterministic pages), and OrderBy with expensive keys (ToString/allocations per comparison).
technicalConversation: Ask why their paged API sometimes repeats rows — nondeterministic ORDER BY without a unique tiebreak is the classic cause.
interviewFollowUp: Why is LINQ sorting stable but Array.Sort not, and when does that distinction matter?
keyTakeaway: OrderBy once, ThenBy for ties, unique tiebreak for paging. Comparers for custom order.

questionText: How do GroupBy and aggregations work, and how do you avoid common grouping mistakes?
shortAnswer: GroupBy buckets elements by key; each IGrouping<TKey, T> exposes Key + members. Aggregate immediately (Count/Sum/Average) for reports; materialize groups before nested use; in EF, aggregate server-side and watch key translation.
detailedAnswer: Shape: orders.GroupBy(o => o.CustomerId) → groups with .Key and enumeration. Immediate aggregation: .Select(g => new { Customer = g.Key, Total = g.Sum(o => o.Total), Count = g.Count() }) — the report pattern (translates to SQL GROUP BY cleanly). Multi-key: GroupBy(o => new { o.Year, o.Month }) (anonymous composite keys work everywhere). Element selection: GroupBy(k, elementSelector) to slim members. Nested: groups of groups for hierarchies. Mistakes: (1) enumerating groups twice (re-groups — materialize with ToList/ToLookup); (2) GroupBy then per-group DB queries (N+1 — aggregate in the same query); (3) grouping huge in-memory sets without need (ToLookup once, reuse); (4) null keys (allowed — one null group; decide if that is desired); (5) EF key with untranslatable members (precompute); (6) Average on empty (throws — DefaultIfEmpty or nullable overloads). Counting distinct: g.Select(x => x.UserId).Distinct().Count(). Having-equivalent: .Where(g => g.Count() > 5) after grouping (SQL HAVING). Streaming alternative: Lookup for reuse, GroupBy for one-shot queries.
internalWorking: LINQ-to-Objects groups via internal Lookup (hash buckets, one pass). EF binds GroupBy+aggregates to SQL GROUP BY + functions; unaggregated member access may force client evaluation (warning). Average over empty throws InvalidOperationException (no elements) — nullable overloads return null instead.
realWorldUsage: Revenue reports, histogram buckets, error grouping by type, batching by tenant, and test-result summaries.
commonMistake: Double enumeration, N+1 per group, unaggregated EF groups (client-eval warning ignored), Average on empty, and null-key surprises.
technicalConversation: Ask whether their report query runs one SQL statement — GROUP BY in the log versus per-group queries is the check.
interviewFollowUp: How does HAVING map to LINQ, and why must it come after the grouping?
keyTakeaway: Group, aggregate immediately, materialize once. Server-side for EF; Lookup for reuse.

questionText: What is the difference between First, FirstOrDefault, Single, and Find, and which should you use?
shortAnswer: First = first match or throw; FirstOrDefault = first or default (null-check!); Single = exactly one or throw (uniqueness assertion); Find = List/DbSet primary-key lookup (fast path). Default to FirstOrDefault + explicit handling, Single for uniqueness contracts, Find for EF PK fetches.
detailedAnswer: Semantics: First(predicate) throws InvalidOperationException when empty — use when emptiness is a bug (config values, required relations). FirstOrDefault returns default(T) — mandatory null/default check after (the #1 NRE source: .FirstOrDefault().Name without check). Single/SingleOrDefault assert cardinality — Single throws on 0 or 2+ (use for unique lookups: users.Single(u => u.Email == e) doubles as a uniqueness check!). Performance: all short-circuit (stop at first match) — but Single scans to the end to prove uniqueness (O(n) always; First stops early). EF: Find/FindAsync checks the change tracker first (no query if loaded!) then PK query — fastest entity fetch; FirstOrDefault builds WHERE + TOP 1. Predicates inside vs Where+First: identical (Where is lazy). Default pitfalls: FirstOrDefault on value types returns 0/false (can't distinguish missing — use nullable projection or Any first). Async: FirstOrDefaultAsync for EF (never sync-block). Style: prefer TryGetValue/Dictionary for keyed access; reserve Single for asserted-unique domain lookups.
internalWorking: First/FirstOrDefault iterate until predicate true (single pass, early exit); Single continues to detect a second match. Find checks the identity map (dictionary) before querying. OrDefault uses default(T) — null for references, zeroed for values.
realWorldUsage: Config/seed lookups (First), optional relations (FirstOrDefault + check), unique-key fetches (Single), EF entity loading (Find).
commonMistake: FirstOrDefault().Member without null check (top NRE), Single on non-unique data (throws in production on duplicates), Single for performance (always full scan), and Find with composite/wrong key order.
technicalConversation: Ask what their code does when the admin user is missing — throw, default, or degrade? The answer should be deliberate per call site, not habitual.
interviewFollowUp: Why does Find sometimes avoid a database query entirely, and when is that a problem (stale data)?
keyTakeaway: First = must exist, FirstOrDefault = check for null, Single = assert unique, Find = EF PK fast path.

questionText: How do Count, Any, All, and Contains differ in cost and intent?
shortAnswer: Any() = exists? (short-circuits, cheapest); All() = every? (short-circuits on first failure); Contains(x) = membership (hash-fast only on sets); Count() = how many (full walk, or O(1) via ICollection). Prefer Any() over Count() > 0 — same answer, potentially O(n) less work.
detailedAnswer: Cost: Any() stops at the first element (O(1) best case); Count() walks everything unless the source implements ICollection<T> (List/array expose Count property — LINQ uses it, O(1)) — Count() > 0 on a filtered iterator walks the whole pipeline, Any() with the same predicate stops early. EF translation: Any() → EXISTS (stops at first row server-side), Count() → COUNT(*) (full scan/aggregate) — the performance gap is largest against databases. All() short-circuits on first false (vacuous truth: empty returns true — decide if that matches intent!). Contains uses EqualityComparer<T>.Default (O(n) on lists — HashSet for hot membership). Overloads: Any(predicate) beats Where(pred).Any() (one pass either way, but clearer); Count(predicate) similarly. Async EF: AnyAsync/CountAsync/AllAsync. Style: Any() for guards (if (!items.Any()) return;), All() for validation (items.All(IsValid)), Contains for set checks, Count for reporting/paging totals. Null collections: Any() on null throws — guard or empty-coalesce (items?.Any() == true).
codeExample:
if (!orders.Any(o => o.Total > 1000)) { return; } // EXISTS, stops early
// vs orders.Count(o => o.Total > 1000) > 0 — full COUNT(*) server-side

bool allValid = items.All(IsValid); // false at first failure; true if empty!
bool hasAdmin = roles.Contains("Admin"); // O(n) on List; O(1) on HashSet
internalWorking: Any/All/Contains iterate with early exit (no buffering); Count checks ICollection<T>.Count first, else full enumeration. EF: Any→EXISTS(SELECT 1...), All→NOT EXISTS(negation), Contains→IN (or = ANY), Count→COUNT(*).
realWorldUsage: Guard clauses, validation sweeps, permission checks, existence probes before inserts, and paging totals.
commonMistake: Count() > 0 instead of Any() (full walk/COUNT(*)), All() on empty meaning 'valid' (vacuous truth surprise), Contains on big lists in loops (quadratic — HashSet), and Any() on null (NRE — coalesce).
technicalConversation: Ask what SQL their existence check generates — EXISTS versus COUNT(*) in the log is the reviewable difference.
interviewFollowUp: Why does All() return true for empty sequences, and when has that bitten real code?
keyTakeaway: Any/All short-circuit; Count walks. EXISTS beats COUNT(*) for existence. Empty + All = true.

questionText: How do Sum, Average, Min, Max behave on empty sequences, and how do you handle it?
shortAnswer: Sum returns 0 on empty (non-nullable); Average/Min/Max throw InvalidOperationException on empty. Handle with DefaultIfEmpty, nullable overloads (return null), Any-guard, or Aggregate with seed — chosen by whether 'no data' means zero, unknown, or error.
detailedAnswer: Rules: Enumerable.Sum(int) → 0 when empty; Average/Min/Max → throw (Sequence contains no elements). Nullable overloads (Average(int?)) return null instead of throwing — the cleanest 'unknown' signal. Patterns: (1) Zero-default: nums.DefaultIfEmpty().Average() (Average of [0] = 0); (2) Unknown: nums.Cast<int?>().Average() → null → display 'n/a'; (3) Guard: if (!nums.Any()) return ...; (4) Seed: nums.Aggregate(seed, func) never throws (fold with explicit start — also the custom-aggregation tool). EF translation: SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX map to SQL aggregates (SQL AVG of no rows = NULL — EF materializes per CLR nullability; mismatch surprises live here: SQL SUM empty → NULL, but LINQ Sum → 0 — know both). MinBy/MaxBy (by key, .NET 6+) return the element (still throw when empty — same handling). Overflow: Sum(int) overflows silently in unchecked context (use long/decimal accumulators or checked). Performance: single-pass each — combine via Aggregate for one-pass multi-stat, or GroupBy+multi-aggregate in SQL (one statement).
internalWorking: Sum loops unchecked-adding (overflow wraps silently unless checked context); Average divides sum/count as double/decimal; Min/Max track best with a started flag (the flag is what throws when no elements seen). EF binds to SQL aggregates with provider nullability mapping.
realWorldUsage: Dashboard KPIs, gradebooks, cart totals, sensor rollups, and SLA computations.
commonMistake: Average on possibly-empty (runtime throw in production), SQL-vs-LINQ empty semantics mismatch, int overflow in Sum (use long), and Min/Max on empty without handling.
technicalConversation: Ask what 'average order value with zero orders' should display — 0, n/a, or error? The domain answer picks the overload pattern.
interviewFollowUp: Why does Sum return 0 but Average throw, and what does that asymmetry tell you about API design?
keyTakeaway: Sum forgives, Average/Min/Max throw. Nullable overloads or DefaultIfEmpty encode your empty-means policy.

questionText: How do Take, Skip, TakeWhile, and Chunk support pagination and batching?
shortAnswer: Skip(n).Take(m) pages (with deterministic OrderBy!); TakeWhile/SkipWhile bound by predicate (prefix semantics); Chunk(n) batches into fixed arrays. For APIs prefer keyset over offset for deep pages; for processing prefer Chunk over manual batching.
detailedAnswer: Paging: page = query.OrderBy(id).Skip((p-1)*size).Take(size) — OrderBy mandatory (nondeterministic pages otherwise); offset cost grows with page depth (DB scans offset rows — keyset WHERE id > last scales constantly). TakeWhile/SkipWhile: prefix operators (TakeWhile stops at first failure — NOT a filter! Where filters everywhere). Chunk(size): yields T[] batches (last may be short) — bulk insert/export/parallel fan-out without manual counters. TakeLast/SkipLast: tail ops (buffer the tail — SkipLast streams with a queue, TakeLast buffers fully). Range/Index (^1 = last): xs.Take(^5..) slices (Range needs indexable or spans). Async: IAsyncEnumerable supports Take/Skip/Where with await foreach; EF translates Skip/Take to OFFSET/FETCH (SQL Server) or LIMIT/OFFSET. Validation: clamp page/size (1–100 — our API does); negative Skip throws. UI: total pages need a separate Count (two queries — acceptable and standard).
internalWorking: Skip/Take are iterator adapters (counters, no buffering except TakeLast/SkipLast). Chunk fills arrays sequentially. EF: Skip/Take → OFFSET/FETCH with mandatory ORDER BY (provider injects or throws). TakeWhile can't translate to SQL (client-eval or restructure to Where).
realWorldUsage: API pages, infinite scroll, bulk pipelines, log tailing, and prefix-truncated previews.
commonMistake: Paging without OrderBy (shifting rows), TakeWhile-as-filter (prefix semantics surprise), deep offset pages (linear slowdown — keyset), and Count+page in one round trip attempts (two queries is fine).
technicalConversation: Ask how page 10,000 performs on their biggest table — offset scan cost motivates keyset; the EXPLAIN output proves it.
interviewFollowUp: Why can't TakeWhile translate to SQL like Where can?
keyTakeaway: Order then Skip/Take; Chunk for batches; TakeWhile is prefix-only. Keyset beats offset at depth.

questionText: What is the difference between query syntax and method syntax, and when should you use each?
shortAnswer: They compile to the same calls — query syntax (from/where/select) reads like SQL for multi-source joins and lets; method syntax (lambdas) covers everything including operators with no query keyword (Count(predicate), Chunk, ToLookup). Use query for join-heavy shapes, method for everything else; never mix mid-query.
detailedAnswer: Query keywords map 1:1: from→SelectMany, where→Where, orderby→OrderBy/ThenBy, group→GroupBy, join→Join, let→Select-with-anonymous (introduces a range variable without re-computation), select→Select. Anything without a keyword (Single, Aggregate, Chunk, ToDictionary, TakeWhile, MinBy...) forces method syntax — so most real queries end method-style or mixed at the tail (query ... select ... .ToList() is idiomatic mixing at the boundary). Readability: multi-from joins and lets read cleaner in query syntax; everything else is terser as lambdas. Team rule: pick one default (method) and allow query for joins/lets. Transparent identifiers (compiler-generated lets in nested queries) produce confusing errors when broken — simplify to method chains to debug. EF translates both identically (same expression trees). Performance: identical IL modulo style. Style traps: query syntax can't express indexed overloads or custom comparers inline (drop to method for those clauses).
internalWorking: The compiler desugars query syntax to identical method calls (transparent identifiers become nested anonymous types). No runtime difference — purely syntactic. Debugging favors method chains (steppable lambdas); query clauses debug as their desugared forms.
realWorldUsage: Join-heavy reporting queries (query syntax), everyday filtering/shaping (method), and mixed pipelines (query shape + method tail).
commonMistake: Mixing mid-query unreadably, assuming query syntax is SQL (it composes lazily — same deferred rules), and let over expensive expressions without realizing it recomputes per use (it doesn't — let caches per element; but nested lets in EF may duplicate SQL).
technicalConversation: Ask which syntax their team defaults to and why — consistency matters more than choice; joins/lets are the legitimate exception.
interviewFollowUp: What is a transparent identifier, and when does it leak into error messages?
keyTakeaway: Same calls, different clothes. Query for joins/lets, method by default, mix only at the tail.
